   • In open letters, phone calls and group chats, Jensen Huang’s allies are making the case that his ouster as Nvidia CEO was hasty —even as legal scrutiny intensifies.

   • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the call to shut down flights on Friday. Now he’s making his case for more aviation funding.

   • The U.S. attorney in Houston is threatening to investigate congressional Democrats who investigate the Trump administration.

   • Rahm Emanuel is betting America wants a radical centrist as president, writes our chief economics commentator Greg Ip.

   • Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a former Mexican police officer who rose from humble origins to become one of Latin America’s most powerful drug traffickers , has died at 80.

       4. READ IT HERE FIRST   Once bitter rivals, Stephen Miller and Marco Rubio have formed an unlikely alliance.   Marco Rubio was in Stephen Miller’s White House office earlier this month when an aide walked in and urged Miller to check his phone. President Trump had just announced on Truth Social that Miller would become his new chief of staff. Miller turned to Rubio and joked that he was now his boss, and the two men shook hands, according to people familiar with the matter. It was a crowning moment for one of Trump’s longest-serving advisers—and offered a view into the unlikely alliance between Miller and Rubio, who more than a dozen years earlier had been on opposite sides of a bitter fight over immigration policy. Today, their relationship is one of the most under-the-radar—and consequential—of Trump’s second term, report Alex Leary, Vera Bergengruen and Robbie Gramer.

   5.   We talked to job seekers in all 50 states. Here’s what it takes to get hired right now.   American workers live in two parallel universes. Those with jobs are still getting raises and, while angst about job security persists, corporate layoffs are actually down from last year. It’s an entirely different world for the white-collar workers exiled from this fortress. Whether cast out by a layoff or looking for that first job, people are searching longer and harder for work than they have in years. To better understand America’s split-screen labor market, WSJ’s Lindsay Ellis sought to talk to job seekers in every U.S. state. Ultimately, she spoke with more than 100 people, including Jack Weis, whose two-year odyssey after earning a chemical-engineering Ph.D. from Princeton University was featured in a WSJ essay last month.

SEE THE STORY   Hardly anyone shops at this mall—and that’s made it a huge success.     SARA KONRADI FOR WSJ   The owners of the Samanea New York mall in Westbury, N.Y., have turned what was once a collection of fading retail shops into an entertainment emporium, pumping new life into the ailing property. It now attracts families with young children to play laser tag and jump on trampolines. Gen Zers swing on a trapeze or roam the escape room. Couples on date nights visit the axe-throwing bar. The mall’s occupancy has soared to 76% today from 22% in 2019, and foot traffic is outpacing the broader indoor mall sector, according to Placer.ai.

       7. HAPPENING TODAY   • Lindsay Clancy is scheduled to return to court for a status hearing.

   • Earnings: Aramark, Baidu, Tyson Foods

As the AI giant prepares to go public, a wide-ranging group of investors including venture-capital firms, leading technology companies and sovereign-wealth funds are preparing for enormous windfalls. The initial public offering, slated for this week, is expected to value it at $1.33 trillion or more .

       9. AND FINALLY…   Meet the law partner who travels the globe for work—without setting foot on a plane.   As a partner at an international law firm, Scott Segal travels a lot. Already this year, he’s been to Asia, Africa, Europe and Australia. Not impressed? Consider this: The 62-year-old lawyer in Washington, D.C., hasn’t stepped foot on an airplane since 1997. Segal is part of a small but determined group of road warriors who do all their travel on trains, buses, cargo ships and whatever other mode of transportation they can find that’s not a plane.
